studies.label: Online experiment: coffee-mug idea generation with ChatGPT versus Google Search

counts_source.quote: One hundred MTurk workers participated in the experiment. ... Ten participants who failed attention checks were removed. Our final sample comprised 90 participants, with 45 for each tool.

arms.name: LLM (ChatGPT)
arms.description: A custom interface supplied an AI Assistant chat panel using GPT-3.5-turbo through the OpenAI Chat Completion API beside the idea-submission form. It retained recent conversation history and allowed starting a new conversation. Participants were instructed to use the assigned tool and stay on the interface (PDF pp. 9-11, Section 4).

arms.name: Search Engine (Google Search)
arms.description: The same task interface supplied Google Search through the Custom Search JSON API. Participants could browse search results and view selected websites inside the panel (PDF pp. 9-11, Section 4).

studies.task: MTurk participants generated up to five innovative coffee-mug ideas using their randomly assigned tool (PDF p. 9, Section 4).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT, GPT-3.5-turbo through OpenAI’s Chat Completion API
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 9, Section 4 (Experimental Setup); the model release year and dated model snapshot are not stated.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is mentioned in the complete manuscript or Appendix A.

estimates.outcome: Idea Novelty (participant mean of normalized MTurk ratings)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: MTurk lay raters assessed novel, original, and exciting on a seven-point Likert scale. Scores were normalized into z-scores within evaluator, averaged across the relevant three items per idea, and then averaged across each participant’s valid ideas. Both arms were scored on GPT-3.5-turbo summaries of at most ten words, checked against the original ideas by postgraduate students (PDF pp. 12-13, Section 5.1; p. 16, Section 5.2.3).

estimates.notes: One-way ANOVA compares participant-level outcomes. No arm SD, arm SE, difference SE, confidence interval, ANOVA degrees of freedom, or standardized effect is printed for this contrast. Table 2 (PDF p. 17) supplies descriptive statistics across both conditions, not arm-specific SDs or a stated pooled within-arm SD; these are not substituted into arm SD fields. Appendix A gives effects adjusted for post-treatment process variables and is not used for the randomized arm contrast. The printed Difference cell is inconsistent with the two printed arm means. All three numbers are retained exactly as printed; no correction is inferred. Table 2’s Idea Novelty and Functional Appropriateness row labels also appear inconsistent with Table 3. Only participants with a valid idea have scores: this is selection after assignment, not a complete intention-to-treat comparison.

estimates.outcome: Divergent Thinking (semantic divergence of ideas within condition)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Each idea receives one minus its average cosine similarity to all other ideas from participants in the same condition, using OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002. The participant score averages the divergence of that participant’s ideas. The comparison pool is the arm’s ideas, and higher values mean greater divergence. Scored texts are the checked GPT-3.5-turbo summaries, not the original submissions (PDF pp. 12-13, Section 5.1; pp. 16-17, Section 5.2.3 and footnote 10).

estimates.notes: One-way ANOVA compares participant-level outcomes. No arm SD, arm SE, difference SE, confidence interval, ANOVA degrees of freedom, or standardized effect is printed for this contrast. Table 2 (PDF p. 17) supplies descriptive statistics across both conditions, not arm-specific SDs or a stated pooled within-arm SD; these are not substituted into arm SD fields. Appendix A gives effects adjusted for post-treatment process variables and is not used for the randomized arm contrast. This compares different people’s outputs, not only diversity within a person, so it is diversity/across_people. Both arm levels, the raw difference, and the participant-level F test are retained in the paper’s units. Table 3 counts match participants with a valid idea, whereas the definition on PDF p. 17 says tool nonusers have missing scores; the sample is therefore flagged for clarification. The text does not specify whether a participant’s own other ideas or invalid ideas enter the comparison pool, whose size differs between arms. Scores depend on the shared within-condition pool; the paper describes one-way ANOVA and no adjustment for this dependence. Table 2 repeats the Functional Appropriateness row for Divergent Thinking and does not give a usable divergence SD. Footnote 10 states that TF-IDF embeddings yield consistent results but prints no separate arm statistics or test for that robustness variant.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Count of valid ideas per participant, with a maximum of five. Postgraduate screeners excluded ideas unrelated to coffee-mug design and retained duplicate ideas only once. Normally only the first idea in each box counted, but extra ideas could count if not all boxes contained valid ideas. The analysis retains participants with no valid ideas (PDF p. 12, Section 5.1; p. 15, Section 5.2.3; p. 20, Table 3 Panel C).

Divergence of prompts/search queries is an input-process measure, not a score on the submitted creative output (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 5.2.1; p. 19, Table 3).
Measures the amount of content received from tools, not participants’ creative outputs (PDF p. 14, Section 5.2.2; p. 19, Table 3).
Measures task relevance of content received from tools, not participants’ creative outputs (PDF p. 15, Section 5.2.2; p. 19, Table 3).
Measures diversity of tool-provided content, rather than the ideas participants submitted; distinct from the extracted Divergent Thinking outcome (PDF pp. 14-15, Section 5.2.2; p. 19, Table 3).

The ratio of idea sentences copied from tool content is a copying/adoption process measure. It does not assess creativity of an output or similarity across different people’s outputs (PDF p. 15, Section 5.2.2; p. 19, Table 3).

open_items: The Idea Novelty difference in Table 3 Panel C is inconsistent with its printed arm means. The intended values cannot be confirmed from the paper; the printed values are retained without repair (PDF pp. 19-20).

Table 2’s Idea Novelty and Functional Appropriateness summary rows appear mislabeled relative to Table 3, and its Divergent Thinking row repeats Functional Appropriateness. Corrected outcome-specific descriptive statistics are needed; no row swap or SD substitution is made (PDF p. 17 versus p. 20).

Arm-level participant SDs, unadjusted difference SEs/CIs, and ANOVA degrees of freedom are not printed. Appendix A’s conditional-model SEs cannot supply the main contrasts’ uncertainty. No data or code URL is stated (PDF pp. 19-20 and 33-37).
Randomized counts and attention-check exclusions by arm are not reported, so arm n_randomized is null (PDF p. 11).

Novelty and functional appropriateness are analyzed only for participants who produced a valid idea, a condition determined after assignment. The paper provides no full randomized-sample ratings or adjustment for this selection (PDF pp. 12, 16, and 20).

For Divergent Thinking, the prose says that tool nonusers have missing values, but Table 3’s counts instead match the participants with valid ideas. The actual inclusion rule needs confirmation; the estimate uses the printed Table 3 counts (PDF pp. 12, 17, 19-20).

The divergence comparison set is not explicit about inclusion of a participant’s own other ideas or invalid ideas. The TF-IDF robustness result has no separate numerical report (PDF p. 17 and footnote 10).

The reported rater recruitment, workload, average raters per idea, and valid-idea total do not reconcile; the final rater and rating counts and the exact rated idea set need clarification (PDF pp. 12 and 16).
The paper does not state the release year or dated model snapshot of GPT-3.5-turbo; ai_tool.year is null (PDF p. 9).
notes: Extraction completed on 2026-10-10. The full markdown was read in consecutive chunks through the references and Appendix A. Every cited PDF page was independently extracted with PyMuPDF; PDF and printed page numbers coincide. Individual random assignment is stated on PDF pp. 9 and 11 and reaffirmed on p. 23. The five main outcome contrasts are Table 3 Panel C. Participant-level analyses are used, not counts of ideas or raters. The screening form reports no shared sample with another paper. Only the designated extraction file was written. No effects, standard errors, degrees of freedom, or corrected table entries were calculated.
